sections.title: Nodes 0 & 1 — Data in files, and a server that owns the bytes
sections.content:
Where this sits

This is the base of the entire chain, and it is the only node with nothing beneath it. Everything that follows — constraints, indexes, the planner, the write-ahead log, MVCC, vacuum, locking, pooling, replication — is a consequence of one decision made here: that a single long-running program takes exclusive ownership of some bytes on disk, and everybody else has to ask it for things over a network. If you understand why that decision was forced, and what it physically consists of, the rest of Postgres stops being a list of features and starts being a sequence of things that had to happen.

Nodes 0 and 1 are elaborated together. Node 0 is the situation before a database exists, and it only earns its place by making Node 1 inevitable.

Every term, from absolute zero

Data — any information a program holds. A number, a name, a date, a list of bookings. While a program is running, its data lives in the computer's working memory, which is fast and completely temporary: when the program stops, for any reason, every value it was holding ceases to exist.

Persist — to make data survive the program stopping. The only way to do this is to write the data somewhere that outlives the program. Historically and still today, that means writing it to a disk, and the ordinary way to write to a disk is to write a file.

File — a named sequence of bytes stored on a disk. That is the whole definition. A file has no inherent structure; it is a run of bytes with a name and a length. Any meaning — "this is JSON", "this is a photograph" — is a convention agreed between whoever writes it and whoever reads it, not a property the file itself possesses.

Byte — the unit files and memory are measured in. One byte holds a number from 0 to 255, which is enough to represent one ordinary English character. A thousand bytes is a kilobyte, a million a megabyte, a billion a gigabyte. When this topic says a page is 8192 bytes, it means a run of 8192 of those.

Filesystem — the part of the computer that organises files into named directories and keeps track of where on the physical disk each one's bytes actually are. It is what makes /var/lib/postgresql/18/main mean something.

Path — the full name of a file, including every directory it sits inside, written with slashes: /var/lib/postgresql/18/main/base/16384/24601. Later in this elaboration you will look at a path exactly like that one and find your own table in it.

Program — a file containing instructions. Inert until something runs it.

Process — one running instance of a program. The distinction matters here more than it usually does: one program can be running as many separate processes at the same time, each with its own private working memory, none of which can see the others' values. Two copies of your API server running at once are two processes. This is the fact that makes Node 0's first problem possible at all.

Concurrency — more than one thing happening in overlapping time. When your web service handles two requests at once, whether truly simultaneously or by rapidly alternating between them, that is concurrency. It is not an exotic condition; it is the normal state of any service that more than one person uses.

Race condition — a bug whose occurrence depends on the relative timing of concurrent operations. The word "race" is literal: two operations are racing, and which one finishes first decides the outcome. Race conditions are miserable to debug precisely because they do not reproduce reliably — the same code with the same inputs is correct most of the time.

Lost update — the specific race condition where two operations both read the same value, both compute a new value from it, and both write, so that the second write silently erases the first one's change. Nothing errors. Nothing is logged. The change is simply not there. This is the failure Node 0 opens with, and it returns with far more precision in Node 8 and Node 10, where you will be able to explain not just that it happens but exactly which snapshot each transaction was reading from.

Atomic — from the Greek for "indivisible". An operation is atomic if it either happens completely or does not happen at all, with no observable in-between state. Writing two records to a file is not atomic: there is a moment where one is written and the other is not, and if the program dies at that moment, that half-state becomes permanent. Atomicity is the guarantee Node 7's transactions exist to provide.

Flush — to force data that has been handed over for writing to be actually placed on the physical disk. When a program writes to a file, the bytes are typically accepted and held in memory for a while before being written for real, because batching many writes is far more efficient than doing each one immediately. The consequence is that "the write succeeded" and "the data is on the disk" are two different events, sometimes seconds apart. Node 7 is entirely about closing that gap deliberately, with a call named fsync that does not return until the bytes are genuinely durable.

Server — in this context, not a machine but a program: one that starts up, waits, and responds to requests from other programs, for as long as you leave it running. The machine it happens to run on is also colloquially called a server, which is a persistent source of confusion; here, unless stated otherwise, the server is the program.

Client — the program doing the asking. Your API service is a client of Postgres. So is psql. So is any dashboard tool you point at the database.

Network socket — the mechanism by which two programs send bytes to each other, whether they are on the same machine or on opposite sides of the world. From the point of view of both programs it behaves like a pipe: you put bytes in one end and they come out the other, in order.

TCP — the set of rules that makes that pipe reliable: bytes arrive in the order sent, none are lost, and none are duplicated. Every Postgres connection in this topic is a TCP connection.

Port — a number from 1 to 65535 that distinguishes which program on a machine an incoming connection is meant for. A machine has one network address, but many programs may want to receive connections on it; the port number is how the connection says which. Postgres's default is 5432, and it is worth saying plainly that the number means nothing — it is simply what the project registered as its own so that clients would have a sane default to try. It is not derived from anything.

Protocol — the agreement about what the bytes flowing through the socket mean. Both sides must hold the same agreement or nothing works. Postgres's is called the frontend/backend protocol, it is fully documented, and the current version is 3.0, unchanged since Postgres 7.4 in 2003.

Driver — a library that implements the protocol for you, so your code can call a function instead of assembling bytes. In Node.js the two real choices are pg and postgres.js. Node 19 is about the decisions a driver makes on your behalf and where they surprise you.

Database — an unhelpfully overloaded word, used for at least three things. Loosely, the entire system ("we use a Postgres database"). Precisely in Postgres, a named container of tables inside one server, isolated from its siblings. And colloquially, the machine the server runs on. In this topic the precise sense is used wherever it matters, and the loose sense is called "the server" or "Postgres" instead.

DBMS — database management system: the program itself, as a category. Postgres, MySQL, SQLite and Oracle are all DBMSs. Nobody says the acronym out loud, but it appears constantly in writing about the field.

Cluster — in Postgres, one running server managing one directory on disk, containing several databases. It is a badly chosen word, because everywhere else in software "cluster" means several machines cooperating, and here it means very nearly the opposite: one server, one directory. When Postgres's own documentation says "cluster", it means this.

Data directory — the directory that constitutes a cluster. Every byte the server owns lives inside it: the tables, the configuration files, the write-ahead log from Node 7. Its conventional path on a Debian-based system is /var/lib/postgresql/18/main, and it is universally referred to by the name of the environment variable that points at it, PGDATA.

Table — a fixed set of named, typed columns, and an unordered bag of rows. Every row has a value for every column. "Unordered" is a real property and not an oversight: a table has no inherent sequence, and a query with no ORDER BY may return rows in any order at all, including a different one tomorrow for identical data.

Type — the declared kind of a column's values: whole number, decimal number, text, timestamp, boolean. Postgres enforces types strictly, which is the first layer of Node 2's defences.

Tuple — Postgres's internal word for a stored row. You will meet it constantly in documentation and error messages. It is not simply a synonym for "row": from Node 8 onward, one row of your data may be represented by several tuples on disk at the same time, which is that node's entire subject.

Relation — the formal name for a table in relational theory, and Postgres's internal name for anything table-shaped stored in files: tables, indexes, sequences, materialized views. This is why so many built-in functions are named pg_relation_size and pg_total_relation_size rather than anything with "table" in it.

Schema — a namespace inside a database, grouping tables so that two of them can share a name without colliding. Every database has one called public, which you get by default and which is why most people never think about schemas at all until they need per-tenant isolation. Note the collision of vocabulary: "schema" also loosely means "the shape of your tables", as in "schema design" and "schema migration", and that second sense is the one used everywhere else in this topic.

Query — a request sent to the server describing data you want, or a change you want made.

SQL — Structured Query Language, the language those requests are written in. Node 3 is about its single most important property: that it is declarative, describing a result rather than a procedure.

Role — Postgres's unified concept for what other systems split into users and groups. A role with the LOGIN attribute is what you would call a user. Permissions are granted to roles, and roles can contain other roles.

System catalog — the set of tables in which Postgres stores information about itself: which tables exist, what columns they have, which indexes are defined, which connections are currently running. They are ordinary tables queried with ordinary SQL, which is why monitoring Postgres (Node 17) requires no special tooling at all — you just SELECT from them.

OID — object identifier: a four-byte number Postgres assigns to every object it tracks internally, used as the key in the system catalog. You will use OIDs directly in a moment to locate your own table's file on disk.

The history — why this exists at all

For the first two decades of commercial computing there was no such thing as a database in the modern sense. Programs read and wrote files, and every program contained its own code for interpreting the bytes in those files. If a company had a payroll program and a personnel program, each had its own idea of what an employee record looked like, and changing that layout meant changing both programs and converting every existing file. This arrangement was called file processing, and it is worth understanding that it did not merely have bugs — it had a structural problem, which is that the meaning of the data lived in the programs rather than in the data. Nobody could answer a new question without writing a new program, and no rule about the data could be enforced except by persuading every program to enforce it.

The first systems called databases arrived in the mid-1960s and solved that by centralising both the data and the code that navigated it. IBM's IMS, built for the Apollo programme and shipped in 1968, organised records into a strict tree: an order belonged to a customer, and to find the order you started at the customer and followed a chain of pointers down. A rival design standardised by a committee called CODASYL allowed a more general graph of pointers rather than a strict tree. Both worked, both were fast, and both had the same fundamental flaw: the questions you could ask efficiently were fixed at the moment you designed the pointer structure. If the data was organised customer-to-orders and you now needed orders-by-region, there was no query to write; there was a restructuring project. Programs also had to know the physical layout in order to navigate it, so any change to storage broke application code.

In June 1970 a mathematician at IBM's San Jose laboratory, Edgar Codd, published a paper called A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks. It proposed something that sounds obvious now and was genuinely radical then: get rid of the pointers entirely. Store data as plain values in named columns of tables, and express relationships by matching values rather than by following links. An order does not point at a customer; it contains a customer number, and you find the customer by looking for the row whose number matches. Codd's argument was that this decouples the questions from the storage completely. Any two tables can be related on any compatible columns, including combinations nobody anticipated, and the program asking the question need know nothing whatsoever about how the data is physically arranged.

That decoupling is the reason for almost everything else in this topic. Because the query no longer says how to get the data, something else has to decide how — and that is Node 6's planner. Because relationships are values rather than pointers, matching them requires either scanning everything or maintaining a separate lookup structure — and that is Node 5's indexes. Codd did not merely propose a data format; he moved an entire category of decisions out of the application and into the database, and the database then had to grow the machinery to make those decisions well.

IBM built a research prototype called System R to find out whether the relational model could be made fast enough to be practical. It could, and along the way System R produced a query language called SEQUEL — Structured English Query Language — which had to be renamed SQL because "Sequel" was already a trademark held by an aircraft company. Everyone still pronounces it "sequel" anyway. SQL was standardised by ANSI in 1986 and internationally in 1987, and has been revised every few years since.

At the same time, at the University of California, Berkeley, Michael Stonebraker and Eugene Wong were building their own relational system straight from Codd's paper, called Ingres — a name inherited from the geography project that originally funded it. Ingres ran from about 1973 to 1985 and used a query language of its own called QUEL rather than SQL. Its source code was distributed for a nominal fee, so a generation of students learned database internals from it, and several commercial products — Sybase, and through Sybase, Microsoft SQL Server — descend from people and code that came out of that project. Oracle, founded in 1977, took a different route: it read IBM's published System R papers and shipped a commercial SQL database in 1979, before IBM did.

In 1986 Stonebraker started a successor project and named it for what it was: POSTGRES, post-Ingres. The design paper, The Design of POSTGRES by Stonebraker and Lawrence Rowe, is explicit that the goal was not a better relational database but an extensible one. Ingres and its commercial contemporaries had a fixed set of types — numbers, strings, dates — and if your data was a polygon or a chemical structure or a document, you were expected to encode it into a string and give up. POSTGRES proposed that users should be able to add their own types, their own operators, and crucially their own index methods, so that a new kind of data could be searched as fast as a built-in one. That single decision, made in 1986, is why PostGIS and pgvector exist today as extensions rather than as forks, and it is the whole subject of Node 16.

POSTGRES was released to outside users in 1989 and developed through version 4.2 in 1994, at which point Berkeley ended the project. It still used a language of its own, POSTQUEL, which by then was a serious liability because the industry had settled on SQL. In 1994 two Berkeley graduate students, Andrew Yu and Jolly Chen, replaced POSTQUEL with an SQL interpreter and released the result as Postgres95. It was fast, it was free, and people began using it in earnest.

In 1996 the project was handed to a group of volunteers on the internet, renamed PostgreSQL to reflect that it now spoke SQL, and given the version number 6.0 — continuing Berkeley's numbering from 4.2 rather than starting over, which is why there has never been a PostgreSQL 1 through 5. It has been developed by that community ever since, with no owning company, under a permissive licence. Stonebraker received the Turing Award, computing's highest honour, in 2014, with POSTGRES named in the citation.

Two practical things follow from that lineage. First, releases are annual, arriving each September, each supported for five years. The version numbering changed at version 10 in 2017: before that, a major version was two numbers (9.5, 9.6) and the third was the patch level; from 10 onward a major version is one number and the second is the patch. So "9.6" and "10" are each a single major version, and people who learned the old scheme routinely misread "13.4" as a major version when it is 13, patch 4. The current major version is 18, released 25 September 2025; 19 is expected around September 2026.

Second, the name. Officially PostgreSQL; universally spoken as "Postgres"; the project accepts both and its own documentation admits the SQL suffix causes endless pronunciation grief. Nobody will think less of you for saying Postgres. Saying "Postgre" will make people wince, because there is no such thing.

The mechanism — traced

Now the physical account: what actually exists, and what actually happens, from starting the server to getting rows back. Everything below is something you can verify yourself in Stage 1 of slotline.

Starting the server. One process starts, conventionally called the postmaster. It reads two configuration files out of the data directory — postgresql.conf, which holds settings, and pg_hba.conf, which holds authentication rules — then opens a listening socket on port 5432 and waits. At this point nothing is being read from your tables and no query can run. There is one process, holding one directory, listening.

What is in the data directory. Look inside and the layout is legible. PG_VERSION is a text file containing the major version number, so the server can refuse to start against a directory written by a different version. base/ holds one subdirectory per database, and inside each of those, one file per table or index. global/ holds the few catalog tables shared across all databases, such as the list of roles. pg_wal/ holds the write-ahead log, which is Node 7's entire subject. pg_xact/ records which transactions committed and which aborted, which is what Node 8's visibility rules consult. There are a dozen more directories, but those five are the ones that will matter to you.

Connecting. Your client opens a TCP connection to port 5432 and sends a startup message. Its bytes are: a four-byte length; then a four-byte protocol version, which for version 3.0 is the number 196608 — that value is simply 3 in the upper two bytes and 0 in the lower two, so it reads as "3.0" when split; then a run of null-terminated strings in pairs, such as user, devansh, database, slotline, terminated by an extra zero byte. There is no message-type letter on this one packet, because at that moment the server does not yet know which protocol version it is speaking. Every subsequent message from the client does begin with a single letter identifying its type.

The fork. The postmaster does not handle your connection itself. It creates a brand-new operating-system process dedicated to your connection alone, called a backend, and that process serves you for as long as the connection lives, then exits. One connection, one process, always. This is a design decision from the 1980s that Postgres still holds to in version 18, and it is the reason connections are expensive and pooling is not optional — but that is Node 12's argument, and it is mentioned here only so you know that the fork is where it starts.

Authentication. The backend consults pg_hba.conf, a list of rules matched in order on connection type, database name, role name and source address. The first matching line decides the method. The modern default is scram-sha-256, a challenge-response exchange in which your password never crosses the connection in any form, not even hashed — the two sides prove knowledge of it by exchanging derived values. The server sends an AuthenticationRequest message, tagged with the letter R, and a short exchange follows. If pg_hba.conf has no matching line at all, the connection is refused before any password is even considered, which explains a large fraction of "connection refused" confusion.

Getting ready. Once authenticated, the server sends a burst of messages you never see but which your driver reads: a series of ParameterStatus messages (letter S) announcing settings such as the server version, the client encoding and the session time zone; a BackendKeyData message (letter K) containing this backend's process id and a secret, which exist so that a second connection can later ask the server to cancel a query running on this one; and finally ReadyForQuery (letter Z), carrying a single status byte — I for idle, T for inside a transaction, E for inside a failed transaction. Your driver sends nothing until it sees that Z, and it will see one after every completed statement for the rest of the connection's life. It is the heartbeat of the protocol.

Sending a query. The simplest form is one message: the letter Q, a four-byte length, the SQL text, and a zero byte. So SELECT id, starts_at FROM bookings LIMIT 3 travels as roughly fifty bytes with a Q on the front. There is a second, more elaborate way to send queries — separate Parse, Bind and Execute messages, letters P, B and E — which is what your driver actually uses when you write $1 parameters, and which Node 12 covers as prepared statements. The simple form is the one to picture first.

Getting rows back. The reply is a sequence of messages, not a blob. First one RowDescription (letter T) listing the output columns with their names and the OID of each column's type — the client uses those OIDs to decide how to convert the bytes, which is exactly where Node 19's surprises come from, such as a bigint arriving in JavaScript as a string. Then one DataRow (letter D) per row, each carrying the raw field values. Then CommandComplete (letter C) with a short tag such as SELECT 3 — and that number is the row count, which is why an INSERT returns INSERT 0 1, the zero being a long-obsolete OID field kept for compatibility. Then ReadyForQuery again, and the connection is idle.

The whole conversation is that simple, and every client you will ever use — psql, pg, Drizzle, a GUI tool — is doing exactly this and nothing more exotic.

Finding your table on disk. This is the part that makes the abstraction concrete, and it takes four steps. Ask which database you are in and its OID: SELECT oid, datname FROM pg_database WHERE datname = current_database(); — suppose it answers 16384. Ask which file holds your table: SELECT relfilenode FROM pg_class WHERE relname = 'bookings'; — suppose 24601. Your table's bytes are then at base/16384/24601 inside the data directory. Postgres will do the whole thing for you with SELECT pg_relation_filepath('bookings');. Go into the container, list that path, and you are looking at your own rows.

Two details are worth registering while you are there. The number in the filename is the relfilenode, not the OID; they start out equal but diverge, because any operation that rewrites a table — VACUUM FULL in Node 9, some ALTER TABLE forms in Node 13 — writes a new file with a new relfilenode and drops the old one, while the OID stays the same. And the file's size will be an exact multiple of 8192, because Postgres allocates storage only in whole 8 KB pages, which is Node 4's opening fact.

Databases inside the cluster. Each subdirectory of base/ is one database, and the isolation between them is total: a connection is bound to exactly one database and cannot see another's tables, no matter what permissions you hold. Two exist from the start. template1 is the pattern from which CREATE DATABASE copies — anything you install into it appears in every database you create afterwards, which is occasionally useful and occasionally a nasty surprise. template0 is a pristine copy that is never modified, kept so that you always have a clean pattern to fall back on and so that dumps can be restored into a known-empty database.

Schemas and name resolution. Inside a database, every table lives in a schema, and when you write an unqualified name like bookings the server resolves it by walking a list called search_path, which defaults to "$user", public. That means it looks for a schema named after your role first, then public. Fully qualified, your table is slotline.public.bookings. This stays quiet until the moment it does not — a per-tenant schema layout, or an extension that installs its objects into a schema of its own, both make search_path suddenly load-bearing.

psql, and the fact that nothing is magic. psql is a client like any other, and its \d commands are not protocol features but ordinary SQL queries against the system catalog — which you can prove immediately. Start it with psql -E and every meta-command prints the SQL it issues before running it. Type \dt and watch it emit a join of pg_class against pg_namespace filtering on relation kind. This is worth doing once and remembering forever, because it establishes the pattern for all of Node 17: the server's own state is just tables, and anything a tool can show you, you can query directly.

In your project

Stage 1 of slotline is this node made physical. You bring up Postgres 18 in Docker, write the migration runner yourself in about fifty lines, and then spend the rest of the stage in psql attacking your own schema — inserting a booking for a resource that does not exist, a negative price, a status of 'banana' — and reading each rejection properly. The reason that exercise belongs in Stage 1 rather than later is exactly Node 0's fourth failure: in a world of files, none of those insertions could be prevented, and every reader of the data would have to defend against them forever.

Two specific investigations belong here and are cheap while you are already inside. First, run the four-step file hunt above and look at your own bookings file in the container; you will come back to it in Stage 4, where you check that relpages multiplied by 8192 matches its size. Second, run psql -E and capture what \dt and \d bookings actually send — that transcript is a good first entry for docs/, and it is the moment the system catalog stops being an abstraction.

One thing to notice as you write the migration runner: each migration runs inside BEGIN and COMMIT, and if the SQL fails halfway, nothing at all is left behind — not a partially created table, not a half-added column. That is transactional DDL, it is a property of Postgres rather than of your runner, and most databases cannot do it. You are relying on Node 7 before you have read Node 7. Notice it now, so that when you reach that node it lands as an explanation rather than as news.

In qbank

qbank connects to Postgres through Drizzle, which connects through a driver, which does exactly the byte exchange traced above — startup packet, authentication, ReadyForQuery, then Parse/Bind/Execute for every parameterised query. Nothing in that path is different because an ORM is present; the ORM's entire job is to produce the SQL text and the parameter list that go into those messages.

The specific gap this node closes is the connection string. qbank has one, of the form postgres://user:password@host:5432/dbname, and it has probably read as a single opaque token. It is not: it is five separate things, each of which appears at a named point in the exchange above. The role name and the database name are literally two of the key/value pairs in the startup packet. The host and port choose which listening socket to open. The password is consumed by the SCRAM exchange and never crosses the wire. Being able to point at each part of that string and say which message it becomes is a small thing, but it is the difference between configuration you copied and configuration you understand.

Worth doing once, since it takes two minutes: point psql at qbank's own database with that same connection string and run \dt. Those are the tables Drizzle created, described by the server rather than by your TypeScript.

What an interviewer does with this

"Why use a database instead of just writing to files?" An opener, often for junior roles, and the weak answer is "because it's faster" or "because it's structured" — both vague enough to sound memorised. The strong answer names concrete failures: concurrent writers lose each other's updates with no error; a crash mid-write leaves a file that is neither the old state nor the new; finding one record among ten million means reading all ten million; there is no way to enforce that a value is present or that a reference points at something real; and there is no way to make two changes happen together or not at all. Then, to land it: each of those maps to a specific mechanism — MVCC, the write-ahead log, indexes, constraints, transactions.

"What happens when your application connects to Postgres?" Asked to find out how deep the model goes. A weak answer stops at "it opens a connection and sends queries". A strong one is the trace: TCP to port 5432, a startup packet carrying the role and database names, the postmaster forking a dedicated process for that connection, authentication driven by pg_hba.conf, then a stream of typed messages with ReadyForQuery between statements. The detail that earns credit is the fork, because most candidates have never heard of it and it is the direct reason pooling exists.

"What's the difference between a database, a schema and a table?" Small, and asked more often than you would expect, because it separates people who have read documentation from people who have only used an ORM. A cluster contains databases; a database contains schemas; a schema contains tables; a connection attaches to exactly one database and cannot see another's data. Mentioning that "schema" also means "the shape of your tables" in everyday speech, and distinguishing the two senses, reads as fluency rather than pedantry.

"Why is it called PostgreSQL?" An icebreaker, but a cheap opportunity. Berkeley, 1986, Stonebraker, successor to Ingres — post-Ingres. Originally spoke QUEL, then POSTQUEL; SQL was added by two students in 1994 as Postgres95; renamed in 1996 and handed to a volunteer community, which is why there is no company behind it. Thirty seconds, and it signals that you read about the tools you use rather than only using them.

"Is Postgres single-threaded?" A question people answer badly. The answer is neither yes nor no as asked: Postgres serves many connections concurrently, but it does so by running a separate process per connection rather than multiple threads inside one process, and since version 9.6 an individual query can additionally recruit parallel worker processes. The follow-up is always about what that costs, and that is Node 12.

sections.title: Node 2 — The database as the last line of defence: types and constraints
sections.content:
Where this sits

Node 1 gave you a server that owns the bytes and will store whatever you hand it. This node is about making it refuse. It is the first node where you make design decisions that you will have to live with, and it is the one whose consequences reach furthest: the types you pick here decide how large your tables are in Node 4 and whether the migration in Node 13 rewrites a hundred million rows; the constraints you declare here are enforced through the indexes of Node 5 and the row locks of Node 11; and the argument this node makes — that a rule in the database is true while a rule in application code is a hope — is the same argument that returns as an exclusion constraint in Stage 3 and as row-level security in Node 15.

Every term, from absolute zero

Invariant — a statement about your data that is true at every moment, no matter what happened before. "Every booking belongs to a resource that exists." "No price is negative." The word comes from mathematics and means simply "does not vary". The whole of this node is about moving invariants out of your head and into the server.

Constraint — a declared rule the database will enforce, rejecting with an error any change that would break it. A constraint is how an invariant gets written down in a form the server understands.

Data integrity — the umbrella term for "the data is not nonsense". It splits into a few named kinds you will hear in interviews: domain integrity (each value is a legal value for its column), entity integrity (every row is identifiable and no key is missing), and referential integrity (every reference points at something that exists).

Type — the declared kind of a column's values. It is two things at once, and people usually notice only the first: it decides what values are allowed, and it decides how those values are physically stored — how many bytes, in what layout, and therefore how large your table is and how fast it is to read.

Strict typing — the property that a value of the wrong type is an error rather than being silently converted. Postgres is strict: inserting 'banana' into an integer column fails. This is worth naming because the alternative genuinely exists — older MySQL configurations would store zero and carry on, and MongoDB will store whatever shape you give it — and people arriving from those find Postgres's strictness surprising rather than reassuring at first.

Coercion — an automatic conversion between types where the conversion is unambiguous and lossless, such as an integer used where a numeric is expected. Postgres coerces where it is safe and refuses where it is not, which is a different policy from JavaScript's, where nearly everything converts to nearly everything.

Fixed-width and variable-width — a type is fixed-width if every value takes the same number of bytes (an integer is always 4, a timestamptz always 8), and variable-width if it depends on the value (a text value takes roughly as many bytes as it has characters, plus a small length header). The distinction matters in Node 4, where fixed-width columns get aligned on byte boundaries and can waste padding.

text — Postgres's string type, of unlimited length in practice. Use it by default.

varchar(n) — the same type with a maximum length check attached. "varchar" is short for "varying character". It is not faster than text and does not save space; it is a constraint wearing a type's clothes.

char(n) — a fixed-length string that pads shorter values with trailing spaces to reach length n. It exists for historical compatibility and has essentially no modern use.

numeric (also spelled decimal) — an exact decimal number, stored as a sequence of decimal digits rather than as a binary approximation. It can be declared with precision and scale: numeric(10,2) means at most ten digits in total, two of them after the decimal point. Arithmetic on it is exact and slower than on binary types.

float8 (also double precision) — a binary floating-point number, eight bytes, following the IEEE 754 standard. Fast, compact, and approximate. It cannot represent the value 0.1 exactly, for the same reason base ten cannot represent one third exactly, and the small errors accumulate across additions.

integer — a whole number in four bytes, ranging from −2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647. That upper bound is 231−1: four bytes is 32 bits, one is spent on the sign, and 231 is a little over 2.1 billion.

bigint — a whole number in eight bytes, up to 9,223,372,036,854,775,807, which is 263−1 and is about 9.2 quintillion. There is no realistic workload that exhausts it.

smallint — two bytes, up to 32,767. Rarely worth the trouble; the four bytes you save are usually eaten by alignment padding anyway.

boolean — true, false, or NULL. One byte.

Epoch — a fixed reference instant from which times are counted. Postgres counts microseconds from midnight on 1 January 2000, which is unusual; the more famous Unix epoch is 1 January 1970. Neither is visible to you in normal use, but knowing that a timestamp is fundamentally one number explains why it takes exactly eight bytes and why comparing two of them is cheap.

UTC — Coordinated Universal Time, the single global reference time from which every local time is an offset. It has no daylight saving. It is the only sane thing to store.

timestamp — a date and a time of day, with no indication of where in the world it applies. Eight bytes. Two timestamp values cannot be meaningfully compared unless you happen to know, from outside the data, that they refer to the same place.

timestamptz — the same eight bytes, but understood as an absolute instant. On input Postgres converts whatever you give it to UTC using the session's time zone; on output it converts back to the session's time zone for display. Despite the name it does not store a time zone, which is the single most misleading name in the whole system and is unpacked properly below.

date and time — a calendar day with no time, and a time of day with no date. Four and eight bytes.

interval — a duration, such as '7 days' or '1 month'. Calendar-aware, so adding one month to 31 January gives 28 February rather than a fixed number of seconds later.

uuid — a 128-bit (16-byte) identifier, written as 36 characters with hyphens, generated so that collisions are effectively impossible without any central coordinator. Node 14 covers the versions and their trade-offs.

NULL — the marker for unknown. Not zero, not empty string, not false, not "missing on purpose". Everything strange about it follows from that one word.

Three-valued logic — because a comparison against an unknown value cannot be true or false, SQL's logic has a third outcome: unknown. A WHERE clause returns a row only when its condition is true, so unknown behaves like false for filtering — but not for negation, since NOT unknown is still unknown.

NOT NULL — a constraint declaring that a column must always have a value.

CHECK — a constraint holding an arbitrary true/false expression that must not be false for any row. It can see only the row being written; it cannot look at other rows or other tables.

UNIQUE — a constraint declaring that no two rows share a value in the given column or combination of columns.

Key — a column or set of columns whose values identify a row.

PRIMARY KEY — the declared identity of a row: UNIQUE and NOT NULL together, plus the statement that this is how rows of this table are referred to. A table has at most one.

Natural key — a key made of real data with meaning of its own: an email address, a passport number, an ISBN.

Surrogate key — a key made of a meaningless generated value, invented purely to be an identifier: an auto-incrementing number, a UUID.

Composite key — a key made of more than one column together, such as (post_id, tag_id) on a join table.

FOREIGN KEY — a constraint declaring that the values in this table's column must exist as a key in another table. The table doing the pointing is the referencing or child table; the one pointed at is the referenced or parent.

Referential action — what should happen to the children when a referenced parent row is deleted or its key updated: RESTRICT or NO ACTION (refuse), CASCADE (delete the children too), SET NULL, SET DEFAULT.

Sequence — a small standalone database object holding a counter, with a function nextval that hands out the next number. Deliberately outside transactions, for reasons explained below.

Identity column — a column whose values come from a sequence automatically. The modern SQL-standard spelling is GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY; the older Postgres-specific shorthand is SERIAL.

DEFAULT — an expression supplying a value when an INSERT does not mention the column.

Domain — a named reusable type built from an existing type plus constraints, so a rule can be declared once and applied to many columns.

DDL — Data Definition Language: the statements that change the shape of the database rather than its contents. CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE, DROP TABLE. Contrast with DML, Data Manipulation Language: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE.

Deferrable constraint — a constraint checked at the end of the transaction rather than at the moment of each statement, so that a temporarily inconsistent intermediate state is permitted as long as it is resolved before commit.

The history — why this exists at all

The systems Node 1 described — IMS and the CODASYL databases — got integrity almost for free, and understanding why makes it obvious what Codd's model had to invent. In a pointer-based database, an order did not refer to a customer by number; it was physically linked to one. You could not create an order that pointed at a nonexistent customer, because there was nothing to point at. Referential integrity was a property of the storage structure.

Codd's 1970 model threw the pointers away and replaced them with matching values, which bought all the flexibility described in Node 1 and lost that guarantee completely. A customer number in an order row is just a number. Nothing about it knows or cares whether a customer with that number exists. So the relational model needed to declare the integrity that the old model had structurally, and Codd knew it: his original paper discusses consistency, and his 1979 follow-up, Extending the Database Relational Model to Capture More Meaning, formalises the two rules still taught by those names — entity integrity, that no part of a primary key may be NULL, and referential integrity, that every foreign key value must match an existing primary key or be entirely NULL.

The standards took a while to catch up. SQL-86, the first standard, had essentially no constraint support to speak of. SQL-89 added PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY and a basic CHECK. SQL-92 fleshed out referential actions, deferrable constraints, and a feature called ASSERTION for multi-table constraints — which was so hard to implement efficiently that essentially no database has ever shipped it, Postgres included. That gap is worth knowing: a constraint spanning several rows or several tables is not something SQL gives you declaratively, which is why Node 10's isolation levels and Node 11's locks exist to protect exactly those invariants by other means.

Where NULL came from, and why people are still angry about it. Codd introduced NULL to represent missing information, and it is the most contested decision in the history of the field. Chris Date, one of the model's leading expositors, spent decades arguing that three-valued logic is a mistake and that missing information should be modelled by decomposing tables instead. Codd himself later proposed two kinds of null — "missing but applicable" and "missing and inapplicable" — which nobody implemented. The practical residue for you is that NULL's behaviour is not intuitive because it is not a value; it is an admission of ignorance wearing a value's position, and every surprise it produces comes from that.

Where the string types came from. char(n) is a fossil of fixed-record-length storage: in the era of punched cards and COBOL's PIC X(20), every record occupied identical space, so a twenty-character field was twenty characters and padding was how you got there. varchar(n) arrived to stop wasting that space while keeping a declared maximum. Postgres, from the POSTGRES project's extensible-type lineage, simply implemented a variable-length string type with no limit — text — and then implemented varchar(n) on top of it as the same storage plus a length check. That is why the performance folklore is wrong: there is nothing to be faster.

Where the floating-point problem came from. IEEE 754, standardised in 1985, represents numbers as a binary fraction times a power of two. That is a perfect fit for measured quantities and a bad fit for money, because 0.1 has no exact finite binary representation, exactly as one third has no exact finite decimal one. Add 0.1 to itself ten times in a floating-point type and you do not get 1. The reason this matters more in a database than in a script is duration: a rounding error in a calculation is a wrong answer once, but a rounding error stored in a column is a wrong answer forever, compounding through every subsequent sum.

Where timestamptz's terrible name came from. The SQL standard defines TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE, and a reasonable reading of the standard is that such a value should carry its offset around with it — which is what Oracle does. Postgres implemented something more useful and kept the standard's name: it converts to UTC on input, stores eight bytes representing an absolute instant, and converts back to the session's zone on display. So the type named "with time zone" is precisely the one that discards the time zone, and the type named "without time zone" is the one that retains an ambiguous local reading. The names are backwards relative to what they do, this is acknowledged in the Postgres documentation and wiki as a wart they cannot fix without breaking everyone, and the only defence is to know it cold. Use timestamptz.

Where identity columns came from. Postgres has had sequences since the Berkeley days, and SERIAL as shorthand for wiring one to a column. But SERIAL is Postgres-specific and slightly leaky — it is a macro, not a type, and the sequence it creates has ownership rules that surprise people during dumps and permission grants. The SQL standard defined GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY in SQL:2003, and Postgres implemented it in version 10 (2017). Both work; identity is the better spelling for new tables, and you will meet SERIAL constantly in existing code and in tutorials.

The mechanism — traced

Constraints are not one mechanism. They are four quite different mechanisms wearing the same word, and the differences explain almost every practical question about their cost.

Types are checked at parse and input time. Every type in Postgres is a row in the catalog table pg_type, carrying its OID, its storage length (typlen, which is −1 for variable-length types), its alignment requirement, and the names of the functions that convert between its text form and its internal bytes. When you send INSERT INTO bookings (price) VALUES ('12.50'), the server looks up the column's type OID in pg_attribute, calls that type's input function on your text, and either gets bytes back or gets an error. Nothing is stored until that succeeds. This is also where extensibility lives: adding a type, as pgvector does in Node 16, means adding a row to pg_type and a pair of conversion functions.

NOT NULL is a flag, and NULL costs almost nothing to store. The rule itself is a single boolean, attnotnull, on the column's row in pg_attribute, checked as the tuple is assembled. The storage side is more interesting: a NULL value occupies no bytes at all in the row. Every tuple that contains at least one NULL carries a null bitmap immediately after its header — one bit per column, saying which are null — and null columns are simply absent from the data that follows. That is why a wide table full of nulls is much smaller than it looks, and it is a detail you will be able to see for yourself in Node 4.

CHECK is a stored expression, evaluated per row. The constraint lives in pg_constraint with contype = 'c', holding a parsed expression tree. Before each insert or update the expression is evaluated against the new row, and the row is rejected if the result is false. Note the precision of that: rejected if false, not "accepted only if true". A check that evaluates to unknown — which is what happens when any input is NULL — passes. So CHECK (price > 0) happily accepts a NULL price, because "unknown is greater than zero" is unknown, not false. This is the specific trap the project spec warns you about in Stage 1, and the fix is to pair every check with a NOT NULL, or to write the check to handle it explicitly.

UNIQUE and PRIMARY KEY are not checks at all — they are indexes. This is the most important mechanical fact in the node. When you declare a column unique, Postgres creates a unique index on it, and uniqueness is enforced as a side effect of inserting into that index: the insert walks to the position where the value belongs and fails if a live entry is already there. There is no separate rule being evaluated. Three consequences follow immediately. First, a unique constraint always costs you an index, with all of Node 5's write overhead and disk usage, whether or not you wanted one for querying. Second, you get the lookup performance of that index for free, which is why looking up a user by primary key is fast without you doing anything. Third — and this is the useful one — because a raw CREATE UNIQUE INDEX can do things a declared constraint cannot, you can express rules the constraint syntax has no words for: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON users (email) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL enforces uniqueness only among live rows, which is exactly what soft deletion needs and which no UNIQUE declaration can say.

FOREIGN KEY is implemented with triggers. Postgres enforces referential integrity by creating hidden system triggers on both tables. On the child, an insert or update fires a check that the referenced parent row exists — and to hold it steady for the duration, that check takes a light row lock on the parent (a FOR KEY SHARE lock, which is Node 11's weakest mode and exists precisely for this). On the parent, a delete or key update fires a check that looks for referencing children and then applies the referential action. Three things follow. It costs on every write, not only on the ones you are thinking about. A parent delete must find the children, so if bookings.resource_id has no index, deleting one resource scans the whole bookings table — and Postgres does not create that index for you, only the one on the parent's key, which already existed. And because the enforcement is a trigger, it can be made DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED, so the check runs at commit instead of per statement, which is how you insert two rows that reference each other.

Sequences are separate relations, deliberately outside transactions. A sequence is its own object with its own small file, and nextval increments it and returns the new number. It does not roll back. If it did, every transaction that had drawn a number would have to block every other one until it finished, because the counter's next value could not be known while an earlier draw might yet be returned — which would turn the sequence into a global bottleneck on every insert. The price of that decision is gaps: a rolled-back insert consumes its number permanently, and so does a crash. Your identifiers will have holes in them, this is correct behaviour, and any code that treats id ranges as row counts is wrong. There is also a per-session cache, so a session that requests numbers in blocks will produce values out of order relative to another session.

Defaults are stored expressions applied at insert time. A column default lives in pg_attrdef. When an insert omits the column, the expression is evaluated then. That timing is why DEFAULT now() gives the transaction's start time rather than the moment the table was created, and it is why Node 13 draws a hard line between a constant default and a volatile one: since Postgres 11, adding a column with a constant default writes the value once into the catalog and hands it back on read for rows that predate it, while a volatile default like gen_random_uuid() must produce a distinct value per row and therefore rewrites the entire table.

Seeing all of it. \d bookings in psql prints the columns with their types, nullability and defaults, then the indexes, then the check constraints, then the foreign keys in both directions. Underneath, that is a set of queries against pg_attribute, pg_constraint, pg_index and friends, which you can run yourself — SELECT conname, contype, pg_get_constraintdef(oid) FROM pg_constraint WHERE conrelid = 'bookings'::regclass; lists every constraint on a table with its definition rendered back as SQL. The contype letters are worth recognising: c check, u unique, p primary key, f foreign key, x exclusion — that last one being what Stage 3 adds.

The design decisions, and how to defend them

Use text. Reach for varchar(n) only when the limit is a real business rule you would want enforced — a country code that must be two characters — and understand that you are adding a constraint, not choosing a storage strategy. The practical argument for text is that changing your mind later is free in one direction and not the other: widening a varchar is a catalog change, but narrowing it scans the table.

Use numeric for money. Always, without exception, including for things that are money-adjacent like tax rates and discount percentages that get multiplied by money. There is a money type in Postgres; do not use it, because it has a fixed fractional precision determined by a server setting and no currency awareness, which makes it worse than numeric at the one job its name claims. If you want to be maximally safe, store minor units — pence, cents — as a bigint, which is what payment providers do; numeric(12,2) is the more readable choice and is entirely defensible.

Use timestamptz for every point in time. An event that happened has an instant, and that instant is the same instant everywhere; storing it as a local wall-clock reading throws away the information needed to compare it with anything. Plain timestamp is correct in exactly one situation: when the value genuinely is a local reading with no instant attached — "the studio opens at 09:00, whatever the date and wherever you are". A booking's start time is not that; it is an instant. Note that the session's TimeZone setting affects display and input interpretation but never storage, so two clients in different countries reading the same row see the same moment rendered differently, which is exactly right.

Use bigint for surrogate keys. The four bytes you save with integer are not worth the migration. Running out at 2.1 billion is not hypothetical for event, log and job tables, and the fix — changing the column type on a live table — rewrites every row under an exclusive lock, which Node 13 will show you is among the most painful things you can do to a running system. Choose the eight bytes on day one.

Prefer a text column with a CHECK over an ENUM for status columns. Both enforce the same rule. The enum is more compact and self-documenting; the check is trivially alterable. The asymmetry is in removal: adding a value to an enum is easy, but removing one requires recreating the type and rewriting every column that uses it, and enums have historically had awkward transactional behaviour when adding values. Status vocabularies change more often than people expect, so the check usually wins. A third option — a lookup table with a foreign key — is right when the set is data rather than code: user-editable, or carrying attributes of its own like a display label or a sort order.

Prefer surrogate keys. Natural keys are appealing until the natural thing changes: people change email addresses, a supplier reissues a product code, a country splits. When identity changes, every foreign key referencing it must change too, and every external system holding that identifier is now wrong. A meaningless surrogate cannot become incorrect, because it never claimed to mean anything. Keep the natural key as a UNIQUE column, where it belongs, and reference the surrogate.

Be deliberate about referential actions. ON DELETE CASCADE is the right default for genuine ownership — a booking's line items have no independent existence — and dangerous everywhere else, because one DELETE can silently remove an unbounded amount of data across many tables and take a long time doing it. RESTRICT is the right default when the child has meaning of its own, and forcing the caller to deal with the children explicitly is a feature. Whichever you choose, write it down: leaving it implicit means the reviewer has to remember what the default is.

NULL, in detail, because it is where the quiet bugs live

Every surprise below is the same surprise: NULL means unknown, and a comparison involving an unknown yields unknown rather than true or false.

NULL = NULL is not true. It is unknown — two things you do not know might or might not be equal. So you must write IS NULL, and WHERE col = NULL is not an error, it simply matches nothing. If you want an equality test that treats nulls as equal, that is IS NOT DISTINCT FROM.

WHERE status != 'cancelled' silently drops every row where status is NULL. This is the most common form of the bug in real code, and it is invisible because the query works and returns plausible rows. The fix is WHERE status IS DISTINCT FROM 'cancelled', or an explicit OR status IS NULL, or — best — a NOT NULL constraint so the case cannot arise.

NOT IN (SELECT ...) returns nothing at all if the subquery yields even one NULL, because "x is not equal to unknown" is unknown for every candidate and the predicate is therefore never true. This one is worse than the others because the failure is total and silent. Use NOT EXISTS, which has no such behaviour.

Aggregates skip NULLs. AVG(score) over ten rows where four are null averages six values, not ten. COUNT(col) counts non-null values while COUNT(*) counts rows, and the gap between those two numbers is often the most useful thing you can learn about a column.

A UNIQUE constraint permits many NULLs, because two unknowns are not known to be equal. Postgres 15 added UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT if you want at most one.

An empty string is not NULL. '' is a known value of zero length; NULL is the absence of knowledge. Oracle famously conflates them; Postgres does not, and code ported between the two breaks on exactly this.

The design conclusion: make columns NOT NULL unless you can say what the null would mean. "Unknown" is a legitimate meaning — a cancellation reason on an uncancelled booking — and "we did not bother" is not. Every nullable column is a branch every future query must handle.

In your project

Stage 1 of slotline is this node end to end, and the stage is deliberately structured so that you design the invariants before writing a line of application code. Every column gets a type you can defend out loud, every rule you can name becomes a constraint, and the stage ends with you in psql attacking your own schema: a booking for a resource that does not exist, a negative price, a NULL where you said not null, a status of 'banana'. Each should be rejected with a specific error, and reading those error messages properly is part of the exercise, because they are the errors your API will have to translate into responses.

Four decisions in that stage are exactly this node's material. The tstzrange column called during rather than a starts_at/ends_at pair — chosen now because it is what makes Stage 3's exclusion constraint possible, and worth knowing you are choosing it for that reason. text plus a CHECK for booking status rather than an enum. An index on every foreign key's referencing column, added by hand, because the mechanism above explains why Postgres will not do it for you and Stage 5 will make you feel the absence. And numeric for prices, never float8.

The difficulty the spec flags for Stage 1 is precisely the CHECK-versus-NULL interaction traced above: your first constraint that fails to fire will be one where the value was NULL and the expression evaluated to unknown, which passes. When it happens, you will now know why in about four seconds instead of forty minutes.

Two forward pointers. Stage 3 is where this node's thesis gets its strongest possible demonstration: after you have failed to prevent double-booking with application logic, and then only partially succeeded with locking, an EXCLUDE constraint makes the bad state unrepresentable — no amount of concurrency, no application bug, and no manual psql session can create an overlap. And Stage 8 is the same thesis applied to access rather than shape: tenant isolation moves out of your WHERE clauses and into row-level security, for the identical reason.

In qbank

Drizzle's schema syntax is a thin wrapper over everything above, and the mapping is direct: .notNull() is NOT NULL, .primaryKey() is PRIMARY KEY, .references(() => other.id) is a FOREIGN KEY, .default(...) is DEFAULT, .unique() is a unique index. Reading your schema.ts now is reading a list of declared invariants, and the useful exercise is to go through it and ask, of each column, "what does the database refuse here?" — and then check the answer against \d on the real table rather than against the TypeScript.

Three specific things to check, all of which are common and all of which this node explains. First, timestamps: Drizzle's timestamp('created_at') generates timestamp without time zone by default, and you have to write timestamp('created_at', { withTimezone: true }) to get timestamptz. If qbank's tables are on plain timestamp, that is a real latent bug and worth confirming either way. Second, foreign key indexes: Drizzle does not add them for you any more than Postgres does, so every .references() in your schema is a candidate for a missing index. Third, key width: check whether ids are serial (a four-byte integer) or bigserial/bigint, and for any table that accumulates rows per event rather than per user — jobs, generations, logs — the four-byte version is a future outage you can prevent today for free.

None of this is knowledge you were supposed to already have; it is precisely the layer an ORM lets you skip, which is why it is the layer you cannot currently explain about your own repository.

What an interviewer does with this

"Should validation live in the application or the database?" A judgment question, and the weak answer picks one. The strong answer distinguishes: the application validates for user experience — specific, friendly, immediate, field-level messages — and the database enforces for correctness, because it is the only place that sees every writer. There is always more than one writer: a second service, a background job, a migration, a person in a shell. A rule in the database is true; a rule in the application is true of the code paths you remembered.

"What's the difference between a primary key and a unique constraint?" Sounds trivial and is a real discriminator. A primary key is unique plus not-null plus the declared identity of the row, and there is one per table; a unique constraint just prevents duplicates, can be declared several times, and by default permits multiple NULLs. The answer that lands is the mechanical one: both are enforced by a unique index, not by a rule engine — which is why they cost you an index whether you wanted one or not, and why a partial unique index can express something neither declaration can.

"Why doesn't WHERE x = NULL work?" Because NULL means unknown, so the comparison yields unknown rather than true, and only rows where the condition is true are returned. Then extend it unprompted, because that is what separates a memorised answer from an understood one: the same rule is why != silently drops null rows, why NOT IN with a null returns nothing at all, and why a CHECK constraint passes when its expression evaluates to unknown.

"varchar or text?" A folklore-detector. They are the same type internally, with varchar(n) adding a length check; there is no performance or storage difference. Choose a limit when it is a business rule, use text otherwise. The bonus point is noting that widening a varchar is a catalog-only change while narrowing it scans the table.

"How would you model an order status?" An open design question. Walk the three options and their trade-offs: an enum (compact, self-documenting, painful to remove values from), a text column with a CHECK (trivially alterable, my usual default), or a lookup table with a foreign key (right when the set is data rather than code — user-editable or carrying its own attributes). Choosing confidently and naming the trade-off is the whole answer; there is no single correct choice and the interviewer knows it.

"Where do you store money, and why not a float?" Almost a freebie, and people still get it wrong. numeric, because binary floating point cannot represent 0.1 exactly and the error compounds across every sum. Mentioning that Postgres's money type is a trap — fixed precision from a server setting, no currency — and that storing minor units in a bigint is the payment-industry convention, turns a one-line answer into a demonstration that you have thought about it.
